newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian polls turn into referendum on reform.
newsitem.headline: Russian polls turn into referendum on reform.

text.p: Weekend elections held to replace two former regional leaders who are now part of Russia's new liberal government looked set on Monday to turn into a stark referendum on the new burst of reform.

Preliminary results of Sunday's voting indicated that second rounds would have to be held in both Nizhny Novgorod and Samara and that the new polls would be a race between candidates backed by the authorities and those supported by opposition parties.
All but the two leading candidates in each poll will be dropped from the second round after no one polled the 50 percent of the vote needed for outright victory in the initial vote.
In the Volga region of Nizhny Novgorod, testing ground for Russian reform since the early 1990s, the candidate backed by outgoing governor Boris Nemtsov came out just ahead of his communist rival.

The election in Samara, another region on the Volga river where reforms began early, put the man touted locally as outgoing mayor Oleg Sysuyev's political successor through to a second round against a man backed by nationalist and liberal opposition parties.
Nemtsov and Sysuyev are both deputy prime ministers in the newly reshuffled, liberal government appointed by President Boris Yeltsin in March.
The votes for their regional replacements are the first tests of public response to the radical reform push set in motion by them and their cabinet colleagues.

First Deputy Prime Minister Nemtsov, 37, is also a strong potential candidate to succeed Yeltsin in the Kremlin and the Nizhny Novgorod vote could give some idea of his chances in a future presidential poll.

Around 100 days on, the new government says it has put Russia on track towards economic growth by taming inflation and interest rates, has ended delays in pension payments, reorganised the budget and made a start tackling corruption.

Its opponents argue that its tough spending and tax policies will cripple the millions of Russians who have already suffered in the transition from communism and who voted communists into power in many regions during a recent string of polls.
Leading political commentator Yevgeny Kiselyov said on NTV's Itogi analytical television programme that the reformers seemed to have underestimated the danger of losing Nizhny Novgorod.

"If a communist candidate comes to power in the Nizhny Novgorod region, which was always considered a bastion of democratic reform, it could become a significant event, a heavy blow not just to the prestige of former governor Nemtsov but to the whole government team," he said in his Sunday evening show.
The second round will be held within the next 15 days.

Preliminary first round results gave Nizhny Novgorod Mayor Ivan Sklyarov -- Nemtsov's favourite -- 41.02 percent and the region's former communist leader Gennady Khodyrev 37.86 percent, local electoral official Pavel Vakhramov said by telephone.

Local television star Nina Zvereva, who was supported by Nemtsov's wife in a family split condemned by Kiselyov, was among three other candidates who polled less than nine percent in the election, in which almost 45 percent of voters took part.

In Samara, first deputy mayor Anatoly Afanasyev, backed by the local administration, was ahead of Georgy Limansky, from former paratroop general Alexander Lebed's party, in the field of 12, Interfax news agency said, quoting local officials.
Leading opposition politicians, scenting a chance to prove the unpopularity of the government's reforms, are making a big effort to boost their candidates' positions.

Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov and ultra-nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky both canvassed in Nizhny Novgorod for Khodyrev while Lebed and liberal opposition leader Grigory Yavlinsky went to Samara to back Limansky.
